h1: Homebrewing in the humid tropics: mould, malt storage and sanitation
title: Homebrewing in the Humid Tropics | Craft Beer School
desc: Mould, damp malt and stubborn sanitation problems: how to store grain, clean equipment and keep ferments healthy in humid, warm air.
teaser: In warm, wet air everything grows: mould on grain, fruit flies on the fermenter. A few habits keep your beer clean.
standfirst: Humidity brings its own problems for a homebrewer: grain that goes damp, mould in corners and microbes everywhere. These habits keep a tropical kitchen from spoiling your beer.
sections:
Brewing malt leaves the maltster at around 4 to 5 per cent moisture, dry and crisp. In humid air it takes water back from the room. Damp malt loses crispness, mills poorly and, in the worst case, grows mould. Once you smell mustiness the grain is finished.

Store malt whole, not milled, in airtight food-grade containers or heavy plastic buckets with sealed lids. Add a small bag of silica gel if the climate is very wet. Mill just before the brew, since crushed malt takes up moisture much faster and loses flavour. Buy only what you will use in a couple of months.

Warm wort is an ideal growth medium for bacteria and wild yeast. The cure is not clever, just consistent. Clean first with hot water and an unscented detergent or a brewery cleaner, to remove soil. Then sanitise everything that touches cool wort or beer: fermenter, lid, airlock, spoon, hydrometer, thermometer and tubing. A no-rinse acid sanitiser is easy to use: mix it to the pack strength and leave a short contact time.

Replace plastic tubing and plastic fermenters once they have deep scratches, because microbes shelter in them. Rubber seals and bungs wear out, so keep a spare set.

Wipe down the brew area after each session and keep it dry. Never leave wet spent grain in the kitchen: bag it and remove it the same day, or compost it. Use a tight-fitting lid on the fermenter and an airlock filled with sanitiser or vodka, rather than plain water, so that fruit flies find nothing to drink and nothing to carry.

Put the fermenter inside a cooler box or a clean plastic tub with a lid if flies are a problem. It also helps with temperature (see homebrewing in a hot climate).

The longer wort sits warm and uncovered, the better the chance for something to land in it. Chill quickly to pitching temperature and pitch the yeast without delay. Many tropical brewers chill with an immersion chiller and an ice bath, then transfer to the fermenter and pitch at once.

Heat and humidity shorten the life of other ingredients too. Keep hops in the freezer or at least in the fridge in sealed bags and see storing hops in hot weather. Use dry yeast where you can, as it keeps better. Keep clean bottles upside down in a closed box so that they do not collect dust and insects before filling.
Fermenting and bottling in damp air

Humidity affects bottling as much as brewing. Caps and corks stored in a damp cupboard can carry mould spores, so keep them in a sealed jar and soak caps in sanitiser before use. After filling, wipe the bottle necks dry. Label with a pencil or a sticker that will not run, since condensation will soften paper.

Bottles that sit warm and damp for weeks often grow mould on the outside. Store bottles in plastic crates with the lids on, off the floor.

If you use a kitchen cloth to cover the fermenter, boil it first or use a clean plastic sheet held with a rubber band instead. Cloths hold moisture and a smell of the last meal.

Humid climates reward routine over heroics. After every brew, rinse the kettle, fermenter and tubing with hot water straight away, before dried wort turns into a film. Once a week, check the grain store, the sanitiser bottle and the hops in the freezer. Once a month, inspect seals, airlock bungs and tubing for damage.

Keep a small notebook with the date, the batch, the fermentation temperature and any sign of trouble. If a batch turns out sour, the notes tell you whether it followed a damp week or a new bottle batch.

A clean tropical brew day is not complicated. It means dry grain, spotless equipment, quick chilling, a covered fermenter and a record of what you did. Our guide on homebrewing in Singapore and Malaysia applies these ideas to a specific climate.

If a batch does turn out sour or odd, a tasting against known faults tells you quickly whether it was infection, heat or a stuck yeast. That skill is hard to learn alone and it is a core part of our Brewing Fundamentals course.
faqs: How should I store malt in a humid climate?
Whole, in airtight food-grade containers, away from the kitchen steam. Mill only what you need on the day of the brew.
No. Mould can produce compounds that are unsafe and will give off-flavours. Throw it away.
What sanitiser is best for a humid kitchen?
A no-rinse acid sanitiser works well and is simple. Clean first, then sanitise, as sanitiser does not work through dirt.
They carry bacteria and wild yeast to open wort and fermenters. A tight lid and an airlock with sanitiser keep them out.
